overview: The L298N is the default answer to 'how do I control a DC motor from a microcontroller.' A microcontroller pin can supply maybe 20-40mA — nowhere near enough for a motor — so the L298N sits between them as a switch, using its own separate, beefier power supply to actually drive the motor while accepting weak logic-level signals to decide direction and speed. Each of its two channels forms an 'H-bridge': four internal switches arranged so current can flow through the motor in either direction, which is how a single driver can make a motor spin forward, backward, or stop. Its main weakness is a real one: the L298N is an older linear (non-MOSFET) design that drops nearly 2V across itself, so the motor never sees the driver's full input voltage, and it can run warm at moderate currents.
simpleSummary: The classic motor driver module that lets a weak microcontroller pin control a much more powerful motor.

specifications.logicVoltage: 5V (onboard 5V regulator available via a jumper, for powering the microcontroller's logic)
specifications.voltageDrop: ~2V dropped across the chip itself — motors run at noticeably less than the supply voltage
specifications.connector: Screw terminals for motor power and motor outputs

pinMap.name: IN1
pinMap.function: Direction control input for Motor A, half of the H-bridge pair.
pinMap.gotcha: IN1/IN2 combination sets direction: HIGH/LOW spins one way, LOW/HIGH the other, and matching states (both HIGH or both LOW) brake the motor.

pinMap.name: IN2
pinMap.function: Direction control input for Motor A, other half of the pair.

pinMap.name: IN3
pinMap.function: Direction control input for Motor B.

pinMap.name: IN4
pinMap.function: Direction control input for Motor B.

pinMap.name: ENA
pinMap.function: PWM speed-enable input for Motor A — feeding it a PWM signal controls speed; tying it permanently HIGH (via the onboard jumper) runs at full speed.
pinMap.gotcha: If the ENA jumper is removed for PWM speed control but nothing is wired to this pin, the motor won't spin at all — a common 'my motor does nothing' beginner mistake.

pinMap.name: ENB
pinMap.function: PWM speed-enable input for Motor B.

pinMap.name: OUT1
pinMap.voltageRange: Up to motor supply voltage minus ~2V drop

pinMap.name: OUT2
pinMap.voltageRange: Up to motor supply voltage minus ~2V drop

pinMap.name: OUT3
pinMap.voltageRange: Up to motor supply voltage minus ~2V drop

pinMap.name: OUT4
pinMap.voltageRange: Up to motor supply voltage minus ~2V drop

pinMap.name: +12V
pinMap.function: Motor supply input (accepts 5-35V despite the '+12V' screw-terminal label).
pinMap.currentLimit: Board-dependent, size the supply for both motors' stall current

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Common ground — must be shared between the motor supply and the microcontroller's ground.
pinMap.gotcha: Forgetting the common ground between the microcontroller and the L298N's power supply is a very common 'nothing works' cause.

pinMap.name: +5V
pinMap.function: Onboard 5V regulator output, active when the 5V-enable jumper is in place and motor supply is 7-35V.
pinMap.currentLimit: Low — enough for a small microcontroller only
pinMap.gotcha: Remove the jumper before feeding in a supply above 12V, or the onboard regulator can overheat.

useCases.title: 2WD/4WD robot car drive
useCases.scenario: Independently control two drive motors' speed and direction for differential-drive steering.

useCases.title: Bipolar stepper motor driving
useCases.scenario: The two H-bridge channels can also drive a single 4-wire bipolar stepper motor directly (with software-controlled step sequencing).

oftenConfusedWith: L293D (lower current, DIP chip form factor)
BTS7960 (much higher current, different control scheme)
oftenUpgradedTo: BTS7960 (for higher current) or a MOSFET-based driver (for less voltage drop and heat)
